THOUGHT: This 69-year-old woman presents with subacute (3-week) headache and progressive bilateral vision loss — a red-flag neuro-ophthalmologic syndrome. Her visual acuity is significantly reduced (20/120 OD, 20/80 OS), suggesting optic nerve or retinal pathology. Although fundoscopy details are not explicitly given, the prompt instructs us to imagine findings suggestive of retinal vein occlusion or hemorrhages — which, in the context of monoclonal gammopathy, raises concern for hyperviscosity-related microvascular compromise. Critically, serum electrophoresis shows a pentameric monoclonal immunoglobulin — i.e., IgM — consistent with Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM). WM is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma characterized by bone marrow infiltration and overproduction of IgM, leading to hyperviscosity syndrome (HVS). Classic HVS triad includes bleeding (e.g., retinal hemorrhages), visual disturbances (blurring, loss), and neurologic symptoms (headache, dizziness, altered mental status). Headache and vision loss are hallmark early manifestations of HVS due to impaired retinal and cerebral perfusion from increased serum viscosity. Her age, absence of systemic B-symptoms (no fevers, night sweats, weight loss), normal calcium and hemoglobin (no evidence of myeloma or renal failure), and pentameric (IgM) paraprotein strongly favor WM over multiple myeloma (typically IgG/IgA, not pentameric) or other lymphoproliferative disorders. Hypertension and hyperlipidemia are comorbidities but do not explain the acute/subacute neuro-ophthalmic presentation. Other causes of headache + vision loss (e.g., giant cell arteritis) are less likely: she lacks jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, elevated ESR/CRP (not provided but implied normal given absence of systemic inflammation), and GCA typically presents with more acute (days) rather than 3-week progression — and crucially, GCA is not associated with monoclonal IgM. Thus, the constellation — subacute headache, progressive bilateral vision loss, IgM monoclonal gammopathy, and presumed retinal hemorrhages/venous occlusion — is highly specific for hyperviscosity syndrome secondary to Waldenström macroglobulinemia.

DIAGNOSIS: Waldenström macroglobulinemia
